content.p: On the morning of Friday 8 July 2022, Shinzo Abe, Japan's longest-serving prime minister, was speaking to a small crowd on a traffic island outside a railway station in Nara when two shots were fired at him from behind. The first missed. The second struck him in the neck and chest. He was 67, and he was pronounced dead that afternoon. Security officers tackled the gunman, a 41-year-old former sailor named Tetsuya Yamagami, who did not run. Japan has some of the strictest gun laws in the world, and the killing of a politician of Abe's stature in public shook a country where political violence of this kind is almost unknown.

Yamagami admitted the killing from the first hearing of his trial. On 21 January 2026 the Nara District Court sentenced him to life imprisonment. He has appealed. The case reached well beyond the courtroom: it exposed the long relationship between Japan's ruling party and the Unification Church, and it ended in a court order dissolving the church's Japanese branch.

Abe was in Nara to support Kei Sato, a sitting member of the upper house who was running for re-election for the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). The race in the prefecture was close, according to the Mainichi newspaper, and party headquarters decided to send Abe back after an earlier visit on 28 June.

The decision came late. The Mainichi reported that it was settled only on the afternoon of 7 July that Abe would speak, and that the venue was moved to the north exit of Yamato-Saidaiji Station at about 4 p.m. that day, less than 24 hours before the event. The head of Nara prefectural police approved the security plan only a few hours before the shooting. Prefectural assembly members interviewed by the paper described the spot as dangerous, because anyone on the road behind the speaker could approach him.

Abe had been speaking for about 30 minutes, according to The Globe and Mail, when the first shot sounded like a large firework. Footage broadcast by NHK showed Yamagami, in a grey shirt and a white face mask, waiting near the intersection. Reuters' review of video found that he was clapping in the background when Abe stepped up to speak.

The Yomiuri Shimbun, citing investigative sources, reported that Yamagami fired his first shot from about seven metres away and the second from about five. Abe turned toward the first shot and was hit by the second. Bystanders tried to resuscitate him; he was taken by ambulance and then helicopter to Nara Medical University Hospital. The BBC reported that he had been conscious and responsive in the first minutes but that his condition worsened. Doctors detected no vital signs on arrival and gave him more than 100 units of blood over four hours before he was pronounced dead at 5:03 p.m. A hospital spokesman told reporters the fatal bullet had been deep enough to reach his heart.

Police said the weapon was handmade and had two barrels wrapped in black tape. Searches of Yamagami's home turned up several similar items, and the BBC reported that police also found explosives there and advised nearby residents to evacuate. Yamagami told officers he had served for three years in the Maritime Self-Defense Force, which he left in 2005, and was unemployed at the time of the shooting.

Within days the focus turned to how a man with a gun had come within a few metres of a former prime minister. A Reuters investigation, published by Al Jazeera, reviewed video, spoke to six witnesses and consulted eight security experts. It found that four bodyguards stood inside the guardrails, that Abe was left exposed from behind, and that there was a window of about 2.5 seconds between the first and second shots. Several of the experts said bodyguards could have shielded Abe in that time. One, Mitsuru Fukuda of Nihon University, called it the "wrong response" that some of the security detail ran at the gunman instead of moving to protect Abe.

The National Police Agency's own review was published on 25 August 2022. Its commissioner general, Itaru Nakamura, told reporters there had been shortcomings in the security plan and in the risk assessments behind it, and that direction from the field commander had been insufficient. The report said the area south of the podium had not been properly guarded, leaving a route open to the shooter. It said that with adequate personnel there, it was "highly probable" the incident could have been prevented. Officers at the scene had not immediately realised that the first sound was a gunshot, which delayed their moving to protect Abe. Nakamura also pointed to a structural weakness, that local police bore sole responsibility for such protection, and announced the agency would take a larger role in planning security for individuals. He resigned that day, which the Asia News Network described as highly unusual for a single incident. The Nara police chief also resigned.

On the day of the shooting, police said only that Yamagami held a grudge against a particular organisation which he believed Abe was connected to. Within weeks the group was identified as the Unification Church, now formally called the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification. In a letter seen by the Associated Press and in social media posts believed to be his, Yamagami wrote that the money his mother gave the church had wrecked his own life.

The trial added detail. His mother, a follower since August 1991, testified for the defence in November 2025, according to the Jiji Press. She apologised for her son's crime and said she gave more than 100 million yen in total. She described donating the proceeds of her husband's life insurance after his suicide, and later selling the family home, because she believed the money would save her elder son, who was seriously ill. At the time, Yamagami was 18 and about to start university.

Yamagami told the court, according to the Boston Globe, that he saw Abe as a supporter of the church and that "striking back at the Unification Church" had become "the very meaning of my life". Japanese media quoted him as saying he took out his anger on Abe because Abe had sent a video message to an event run by a church-affiliated group. In 2021 Abe had recorded such a message for the Universal Peace Federation, praising Hak Ja Han Moon, who leads the church, for promoting traditional family values. A prosecutor told the court that Yamagami thought killing someone as prominent as Abe would draw public attention to the church and fuel criticism of it.

The trial opened at Nara District Court in October 2025. "Everything is true," Yamagami said on the first day. "There is no doubt that I did this." Hearings ran for 15 days, until December. Prosecutors called the murder unprecedented in post-war Japan and sought a life sentence. The defence asked for no more than 20 years, arguing that the church had harmed the family and that the homemade gun fell outside Japan's firearms law. The Boston Globe reported that the court rejected the childhood-hardship argument, saying the defendant's upbringing "did not have a significant impact on the crimes".

On 21 January 2026 Judge Shinichi Tanaka found Yamagami guilty of murder and breaches of the gun-control law and sentenced him to life. Tanaka called the shooting "despicable" and said that firing a gun into a crowd was "extremely dangerous and malicious", according to Reuters, citing NHK. Al Jazeera noted that a life sentence in Japan leaves open the possibility of parole, though many people given one die in prison. Abe's widow, Akie Abe, called the ruling a "turning point" and said she hoped Yamagami would atone. Nearly 700 people queued outside for 33 public seats. Public reaction was divided: the Boston Globe reported that some people saw him as a calculating assassin and others as a figure whose childhood made his act understandable, while Reuters quoted one man who thought he should have been sentenced to death.
In early February 2026 a court spokesperson confirmed that an appeal had been filed. The Osaka High Court is to review it.

The shooting set off a political reckoning for the LDP. In August 2022 Prime Minister Fumio Kishida reshuffled his Cabinet, removing seven ministers with acknowledged church links, among them Abe's younger brother Nobuo Kishi. On 31 August he apologised for the loss of public trust and said the party would cut ties. A party survey released on 8 September found that 179 of its 379 national lawmakers reported links to the church or related groups, from attending events to receiving donations or election volunteers. Its secretary general, Toshimitsu Motegi, denied any tie between the party as an organisation and the church. Opposition lawmakers criticised the survey for leaving out Abe, who was dead, and for not covering local assemblies. The AP noted that Abe's grandfather, Nobusuke Kishi, had helped found the church's political arm in Tokyo in 1968.

The state funeral on 27 September 2022 at the Nippon Budokan divided opinion. Kishida defended it by citing Abe's record and the roughly 1,700 condolence messages received. Al Jazeera reported about 4,000 mourners, with 19 shots fired in salute, protests in central Tokyo, and a Mainichi poll in which 62 percent disapproved. The cost was disputed: the Cabinet first allocated at least 250 million yen, and the government later said it needed at least 1.4 billion yen more, according to the AP, while Al Jazeera cited a bill of 11.5 million dollars. Kishida's approval rating, Al Jazeera reported, fell below 30 percent.

The Education Ministry asked a court in October 2023 to dissolve the church's Japanese arm. On 25 March 2025 the Tokyo District Court granted the request, citing manipulative fundraising. The ministry's evidence rested on interviews with more than 170 people, and the Agency for Cultural Affairs said settlements exceeded 20 billion yen and involved more than 1,500 people. The church called the ruling unjust. On 4 March 2026 the Tokyo High Court upheld the order, and NHK, quoted by The Korea Times, said it was the first dissolution based on illegal acts under civil law. The church lost its status as a religious corporation and a court-appointed trustee began liquidating its assets to compensate victims, though it may continue as a voluntary group. It said it would appeal to the Supreme Court. Hiromi Shimada, a scholar of religion, told NPR that the problem should have been addressed some 40 years earlier, and that few LDP politicians had been held accountable.
